nameStory: The climbing prairie rose gets its name from its impressive ability to scramble up and over other plants, sometimes reaching 12 feet or more as it climbs toward sunlight. Unlike most roses that form neat bushes, this species has long, flexible canes that hook onto nearby vegetation, earning it the 'climbing' part of its name. The 'prairie' connection comes from its native range across the American prairies and eastern woodlands, where it naturally drapes over fences and shrubs.
description: Climbing prairie rose is a vigorous, thorny vine or sprawling shrub that can climb 6-12 feet high when supported by other plants. It has long, arching green canes armed with curved thorns that help it hook onto nearby vegetation. In early summer, it produces clusters of fragrant pink to white flowers, each about 2-3 inches across. This native rose forms dense thickets and is much more of a climber than most other wild roses you'll encounter in New England.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Long, flexible green canes that arch and climb over other vegetation, often reaching 8-12 feet when supported, unlike the more compact shrub form of most wild roses

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Fragrant pink to white flowers in clusters, each bloom 2-3 inches across with 5 petals and a sweet, classic rose scent that's strongest in the morning

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 3-5 leaflets that feel smooth on top and slightly fuzzy underneath, arranged alternately along the stems

idTips.label: Thorns
idTips.description: Curved, hook-like thorns scattered along the stems that grab onto clothing and skin easily - perfect for a climbing lifestyle

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Small red rose hips in fall that persist into winter, about the size of a small marble and slightly soft when ripe

habitat: Look for climbing prairie rose along woodland edges, fence lines, and in old fields where it can find other vegetation to climb. It thrives in partial shade to full sun and adapts to various soil types, from sandy to clay. In New England, you're most likely to spot it in disturbed areas and edges where it has room to sprawl and climb.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge bright green in late spring, and flower buds begin forming on the tips of canes as the weather warms.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs in early to mid-summer with fragrant pink or white flowers in showy clusters. The sweet scent is strongest on warm, humid mornings.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may turn yellowish before dropping, and bright red rose hips develop and ripen. The climbing canes remain green even as leaves fall.
seasonality.winter: Bare green canes remain visible climbing through other vegetation, with persistent red hips often lasting into winter as food for birds.

funFact: Climbing prairie rose is one of the parent species of many modern climbing garden roses - plant breeders have used its incredible climbing ability and cold hardiness to create roses that can scale trellises in harsh climates where other climbing roses would freeze!
confusionNotes: Most other wild roses in New England grow as compact shrubs rather than long climbing vines, making the growth habit your best clue. If you find a rose that's truly climbing and scrambling over other plants rather than standing on its own, you've likely found prairie rose.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'prairie' rose, this species is actually quite rare in New England with only 3 recorded observations, as it's more common in the Midwest and central states. You're much more likely to encounter other native roses like Virginia rose or swamp rose in this region.
compareHints: Climbing prairie rose stands out from other New England roses primarily by its vigorous climbing habit with long, flexible canes. Virginia rose and Carolina rose form neat, upright shrubs typically under 6 feet, while multiflora rose, though it can get large and sprawling, has much smaller flowers in bigger clusters and a more invasive, dense growth pattern.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England roses, multiflora rose is unique for its enormous flower clusters (other roses have flowers in smaller groups or singly) and those telltale fringed stipules.
Rugosa rose stands apart from other New England roses with its unmistakable wrinkled leaves - no other rose species has this corrugated texture.

Among New England's wild roses, swamp rose is unique in its preference for wet habitats - while Carolina rose and Virginia rose stick to drier areas, and multiflora rose (an invasive) has much denser thorns and forms larger, more aggressive colonies.
Among New England's wild roses, Carolina rose is the champion spreader, forming low colonies while relatives like swamp rose grow taller and more upright.
Among New England's wild roses, Virginian rose stands out for its glossy leaflets (rugosa rose has wrinkled leaves) and typically 7-9 leaflets per leaf (most others have fewer).

Among New England's roses, Sherard's downy-rose stands out for its compact size and distinctly grayish, downy leaves - most other wild roses like swamp rose or Carolina rose have greener, smoother foliage.

Among New England's wild roses, smooth rose is unique for its nearly thornless stems – multiflora rose has curved thorns, rugosa rose has dense straight prickles, and swamp rose has scattered thorns along its stems.
Among New England's roses, dog-rose stands out for its large, curved thorns and smooth leaflets without fuzzy coating.
Memorial rose is unique among New England roses for its prostrate, ground-hugging growth habit - all other rose species in the region grow as upright shrubs.
Among New England's wild roses, shining rose is uniquely low-growing and has by far the glossiest leaves.
Unlike the common multiflora rose with its clusters of small white flowers, cinnamon rose has larger, solitary pink blooms.
Among New England's wild roses, prickly wild rose stands out for its extreme thorniness — it has far more prickles per inch than rugosa rose, swamp rose, or any of our other native roses.
Among New England's roses, sweet-brier is the only one with apple-scented leaves - this fragrance alone separates it from multiflora rose, rugosa rose, and native species.
Unlike New England's native roses such as swamp rose or Carolina rose which have green leaves, red-leaved rose's blue-gray to purplish foliage is unmistakable.
